What If You Flew Into a Storm Bigger Than Earth?

Episode 92 of a daily journey through the universe. 🌀
We fly into Jupiter's Great Red Spot: a storm wider than Earth, watched since at least 1830 and maybe for more than 350 years, winds over 400 km/h, roots about 300 km deep measured by Juno, and a storm that keeps shrinking.

segments.text: What if you flew into a storm bigger than the whole Earth?
On Jupiter, there's a storm that's wider than our entire planet. And it has been raging for centuries.
segments.headline: Wider than Earth

segments.text: Astronomers have watched it since at least eighteen thirty. It may be more than three hundred and fifty years old.
It spins counterclockwise, with winds faster than four hundred kilometers per hour. Faster than any hurricane on Earth.
In the eighteen hundreds, it was more than two Earths wide. When Voyager flew past in nineteen seventy-nine, about two Earths.
segments.headline: Voyager, 1979

segments.text: Today it's about one point three Earths wide, and getting rounder. Nobody knows if it will ever disappear.
segments.headline: It's shrinking

segments.text: In twenty seventeen, NASA's Juno spacecraft flew right over it, and measured its roots going about three hundred kilometers deep.
segments.headline: Juno looks inside

segments.text: Why is it red? We still don't know for sure. Sunlight may be breaking down chemicals lifted from deep below.
